utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning ladies and gentlemen. We will have appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues Mr. Turone and Mr. Khan for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can I have the appearances on behalf of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Edina Residovic, appearing on behalf of Mr. Zejnil Delalic together with my colleague Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning your Honours, I am Mr. Olujic, an attorney from Zagreb, Croatia, appearing on behalf of Mr. Mucic, together with attorney Michael Greaves, from the United Kingdom and Northern Ireland.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, Defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic, together with my colleague Tom Moran, attorney from Houston Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning your Honours. I am John Ackerman and along with Cynthia McMurrey we appear on behalf of the defendant Mr. Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Where do we start Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has a number of witnesses it wishes to call. The witnesses are in response to the subpoenas issued by your Honour. The first witness I wish to call is Fadil Zebic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Before that witness comes, may I raise a matter with the Tribunal regarding this witness and others?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may raise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On October 20th, Mr. Greaves and Mr. Karabdic, on behalf of all Defence Counsel, delivered a letter to the Victims and Witnesses Unit. The basic content of that letter was a request that the Victims and Witnesses Unit advise these witnesses upon their arrival in The Hague that Defence Counsel would like to have an opportunity to meet with them and visit with them prior to their testimony, to conduct interviews of the witnesses, since we have not had that opportunity, and no chance to have that opportunity up until now. We received a response back from the Victims and Witnesses Unit. Let me just read you a couple of paragraphs of it: "The content of the letter has been considered and it is the opinion of the Unit that this is a matter which should, as heretofore, be referred to the Officer of the Prosecutor. It is appreciated that time is of the essence as the witnesses will arrive late on this date and are due to commence testifying on 21 October, 197. However, it is considered any intervention such as you have proposed in your correspondence would have an adverse effect on the perceived impartiality of the Victims and Witnesses Unit. Your original letter is returned herewith." They then go on to say they stand ready to assist us in any way they can. The response, to me, is a bit bizarre. These are witnesses that were subpoenaed by this court to give evidence before this court, and it seems to me that they do not belong to any party, but they belong to the list of witnesses to come to give evidence before the court. I am quite certain that the Victims and Witnesses Unit facilitated their meeting with the Office of the Prosecutor, but have taken the position that any mention that we might want to talk to them might affect their impartiality. I think this is totally improper. I think it again shows, as we have seen one time in the past, a connection that exists between the Victims and Witnesses Unit and the Office of the Prosecutor that is improper, because of their announcement that they feel compelled to notify the Office of the Prosecutor that we have made this request. I would therefore ask your Honours that before any of these witnesses testify that they be asked if they would consent to an interview with one or more of the Defence counsel and that we be given that opportunity to interview them before they are called here as witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Niemann, have you any reaction to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is the first I have heard of it, your Honours, and I resent any suggestion that there is any improper relationship between the Victims and Witnesses Unit and the Officer of the Prosecutor. These types of allegations are loosely made, it seems to me, by certain members of the Defence. In any event, your Honours, I do agree that these witnesses are free to be approached by the Defence if they wish. If the witnesses are prepared to talk to them, well and good. But I do say that we have here, in The Hague at the moment, all of the witnesses that we sought to subpoena. We are sitting for three days. The witnesses are very -- going to be very lengthy in the evidence they give. The first two witnesses will not be, but the others will be. The possibility of completing the evidence in the three day period is going to be very difficult, and I must say, just having spoken to a couple of the witnesses already, they are not pleased to be here as a consequence of a subpoena and any delay in the taking of their evidence will not in any way make them any happier to be here, and may affect the evidence that they give. So, your Honours, all I can say is that I certainly do not suggest, for one minute, that the Defence are entitled to ask whether these witnesses are prepared to talk to them. If they are, that is a matter for the witness. But there is a matter of convenience of the court in taking the evidence. In my submission, any delay while these witnesses are spoken to can only be detrimental in terms of the business of the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before any determination is made, may I have the floor, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: My impression was that the Defence had tried to contact them while they were in Saravejo. They refused to talk to us, I think that is what you said on the last occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my learned colleague --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We said if you had any interest before we asked them to come over here, before we made the orders for any subpoenas, you said they refused to have any contact with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as I understood my learned colleague Mr. Ackerman who spoke on behalf of all the Defence, he said only that the Victims and Witnesses Unit informed us that they cannot arrange it for us. Nobody has told us that this wish has been conveyed to the witnesses. Even Mr. Niemann has not confirmed that. That is why we would like this request to be conveyed to the witnesses. And, of course, as we have done in the past, we will respect the will of the witnesses, whether they wish to have any contact with the Defence or not. But that is not the only reason I have asked to speak. I seem to have heard, or at least that was the interpretation, that the Prosecutor informed us that the witness would be here for three days. Your Honours, these are witnesses of extreme interest for the Defence of my client, Mr. Delalic, and I would not like anyone to limit the right of Mr. Delalic to interrogate and cross-examine this witness. I think no witness, including these -- cannot have the privilege of being told for how long they will be here. I think we have never limited the time of the Prosecution for his witness, and we also will avail ourselves of our right to cross-examine the witness for as long as we consider necessary in the interests of the Defence of Mr. Delalic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose you can call the witness, call your first witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please. (10.15 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The view of the Trial Chamber is that the witnesses are here and you might be able to make whatever arrangements you can to speak to them; but the Trial Chamber is unable to postpone their testifying before you have interviewed them. If I understand the request of Mr. Ackerman to mean that while he would prefer prior interview with the witnesses, before they testify, we do not think we can do that. But they are available to you for all necessary cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a couple of practical problems that I need to bring to your attention and put in the record. First of all, these witnesses were acquired at the very last minute, as a result of subpoenas which required them to appear here very quickly after the subpoenas were issued. That gave neither the Defence nor the witnesses time to take any steps that they might have felt important with regard to them being interviewed by us or with regard to any rights they may have, in terms of their appearance here. The second problem is that the only way we could have access to these witnesses is through the good offices of the Victims and Witnesses Unit; and in the letter that I quoted to you this morning the Victims and Witnesses Unit has indicated that they are not disposed to assist us with an effort to talk to the witnesses. We cannot approach them if we do not know where they are, or who they are, and until the Victims and Witnesses Unit has been advised by this Trial Chamber that they should assist us with our efforts to contact and talk with these witnesses we have no way of doing that. So even though the Tribunal has said that we may do that, it is practically impossible for us because we have no idea where they are, or in my case, at least, I would not recognise them if I saw them. That is the dilemma we now find them in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually this is your first application to the Trial Chamber for this purpose. If it was maybe before now perhaps I would have considered how to relay that to you before this testimony. Now they are here to testify. Then you can use the opportunity to ask whatever questions you would want. Okay, you can bring the witness in now. FADIL ZEBIC, (sworn) Examination-in-chief by MR. NIEMANN

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sir, could you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Fadil Zebic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you spend most of your life, particularly your adult life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your employment in Konjic.?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Should I speak about all my jobs, or only the last one I held?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I will make it more specific. What was your employment in the year of 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked for 35 years in Konjic in a number of companies, and the last one I worked for, starting from 1989, was the public utilities company, Standard of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What capacity did you have with that company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a director of the enterprise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long were you director of the company? For what period of time? Until what year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 1989 until 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who became director in 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Emir Dautbegovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the nature of the work of the company? What work did it do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The founder of this company was the Konjic municipality. By its decision it defined the activities within our competence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were those activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To supply the town and surrounding settlements with water, public hygiene in the city and the surrounding settlements, maintenance of parks and greenery, management of market places, and funeral activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in relation to funeral activities, what work was performed by the company? What role did it play? Did it do the whole range of activities from autopsies right through to burials, or was there just a part of that work that it performed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as these activities are concerned, we managed the city cemetery, and we provided the services of transportation and burial of the dead person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would ask you to look at a document I will now show you, if I may, with the assistance of the usher. This is a document that the Defence will no doubt be aware of, but I ask that one copy be given to them because they are aware of it. There is one copy for his Honour. Might the witness be given a copy? Perhaps it might be allocated the next number in order of Prosecution exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document 185.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Zebic, I would ask you to look at that document and just read through it, if you would, please. Mr. Zebic, have you brought another document into court with you that you have before you, other than the one I have just handed to you? What is the document that you have shown there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I went to come here, I took it out of the archives. It has the same number as this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that an original copy of the document that I showed you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you brought that from Konjic with you, when you came this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you compared that original copy with the document that I showed you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have. I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is the copy that I gave you, Exhibit 185, is that an original or a copy of the original of the document that you have the copy for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell me what the document is that I gave you, Exhibit 185? What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the request of the Defence counsel Edina Residovic, in June last year, on 24th June, 1996, we issued this certificate for the services provided in 1992, for some -- in some cases the funeral and transportation and for others only the transportation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is in relation to the people whose names are mentioned on this document, is it, numbered 1 to 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you notice at the bottom of the document it appears to have been signed by someone with the name Kemal Dzajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the director who came from Ornis, another company, in 1994. He came when Emir Dautbegovic abandoned the company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your position in relation to Mr. Dzajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the deputy director and he was in charge of the economic and accounting department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the document that -- you see the signature that appears on the bottom of the document. Did you see that signature being affixed to the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was signed in my presence, and in the presence of Ms. Edina Residovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were there at the time when Mr. Sejic signed the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the information that is contained in the document in relation to the people mentioned there, where did that information come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In order to explain this, I have to say that in 1992 the War Presidency of Konjic's municipality established the wartime assignment of our firm, and the wartime schedule of workplaces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Among the other activities that I listed a moment ago, we were assigned other activities, such as market services, the maintenance of parks; but our main task was to provide water supply for citizens and funeral services. This was determined by a decision of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of 1992, what records did the company keep in relation to its funeral services?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is rather difficult to explain now, because under conditions of war our number was limited. We had only 13 employees. I was in charge, together with a director and the typist, and we had to leave our offices and move to another building, to the cellar of that building, actually to another section of that building, to the basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what records were kept, in these conditions that you have explained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hardly any. In the case of funerals, a record of the victims of the war was maintained by a municipal commission. I think it was called for the Exchange and Burial of Persons Killed in the War. The War Presidency also formed that commission at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So were any records kept of the people that your company dealt with in relation to the funeral services that it provided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For these persons who were killed in the war records were kept by this commission. We only kept a record of the transportation of the body, which my workers, in most cases, never saw; and this transport ended with the delivery to the family, or, as in the case under number 1, 2, 8 and 9, they were brought to the municipal mortuary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know that they were brought to the municipal mortuary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The drivers that performed that activity would inform me, and at that time the mortuary was operational, and the register of dead people was kept, so that we have data stating where and under which number in the cemetery and in which part of the cemetery were people buried. Under the number 1, Zeljko, son of Milana Milosevic, also Slavoljuba Pere Susic, Posko Samoukovic and Zeljko Klimenta. The numbers under 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7, for those numbers, upon the request of Ms. Residovic, we found, on the basis of the memory of certain of our workers, we found the data. But at that time, early 1993, a shell destroyed our vehicle, the funeral vehicle, and there, in a drawer, half burned, remained the book, the register of all orders for transportation. That is how we call it, basically the driver would write down the transportation of a corpse from Celebici; number 3 was in Bradina or in number 4 it was to Donje Selo from Celebici, or from Celebici to Bjelovcina or Celebici to Bradina. The bodies were delivered to the family, or to friends. This was done by my men, together with a member of the municipal commission that I have mentioned a moment ago, and those people kept the Registry. From that book that was burned, we tried to reconstruct something, so we managed to find the workers that did the transport, that participated in the transportation and according to their memory we tried to write that down. It was not really any kind of a notebook or a notepad because at that time we lacked paper, so we simply put together with -- and stapled 30 or 40 pieces of paper, and that is how we kept our registry. So we put that particular certificate in our archives, and then once we have done that we destroyed the actual order for transportation, because at that time we also moved into another building, the building where we were before we had been shelled, and still nowadays we are in this new building. So, for the people who are registered under number 3, 4 and 5 and 6, that is how we established the facts; and the dates were found in the order for transportation. Whether this -- that person had died on that particular day, that is something that me or, that is, my company, cannot affirm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says "transport Celebici Bradina". The reference to Celebici, do you know where in Celebici the bodies were collected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never left my office, that is the cellar, because we only had one telephone and one line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the records suggest to you or indicate where in Celebici the bodies had been collected from, from what you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the basis of this travel order I spoke of, the only locality that is mentioned is Celebici, because we did not use to put in these travel orders where the body came from, not any specified place. They would just mention the town, because simply the transportation fees were paid according to the number of kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not autopsies were carried out on any of these bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in our mortuary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not they were carried out in any other mortuary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it customary for autopsies to be carried out during the course of 1992? I speak specifically of the summer and autumn of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what was done in the hospital, whether they carried out any autopsies, but in our mortuary, we simply did not have the possibility to do that, neither we did any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether any death certificates were issued, particularly in relation to these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We never issued death certificates. In Konjic, what was done in general was if a person died in the hospital then the physician would establish that the person had died, and then inform the family, issue a small certificate, and then the family would go to the municipal department, which I think was called the Registrar of Born and Dead People, and that registry would issue a death certificate. That is how it was done before the war. Whether such documents were issued during the war, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person called, or did you know a person called Simo Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to school together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he die, so far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the nature of his death. I really do not know that, but the burial was an ordinary one. His son-in-law, whose surname was Muftic and whose first name I do not know, I cannot recall, but his nickname was Kina. At that time, he was the member of the HVO. So he came to me, and he registered the death, and he transported him to our mortuary, and asked from us for the funeral services, so we carried out the burial. It was done by our company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend the funeral of Simo Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you attend that funeral, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly. It was either at the end of June or in early July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of what year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I ask you to look at another document. Perhaps that document can be returned to the Registrar, and with the assistance of the usher, I would ask you to have a look at another document. A copy of this has also been made available for your Honours, and one for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You should make copies for the judges also, so we can have a look of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have one, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I did not see a copy of the last document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I made one available for your Honours. It is the same with this one, one copy each for your Honours. There should be an English translation and an original.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we may have been distributed some extra copies of 185.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps the Defence might be able to hand those to your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think we were given the court copies as well as our own. Perhaps we can get someone over here to pass them around.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would ask that the document that I have now --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document of the Prosecutor is marked as 186.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The new one handed to your Honours now is 186. There should be a copy of both. Your Honour should have a copy of both the Serbo-Croat version and the translation in English. I ask your Honours have that in front of you while I am asking the witness about it. I do not believe your Honours have been given a copy of the Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is the certificate of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zebic, the document that you have now been shown, document number 186, looking generally at that document, in your experience of the business that you worked in, in Konjic, in 1989 to 1994, is this a document that is familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, it is the first time I see this document. Secondly, as I have said, just a moment ago, before the war, it is sure that this department, the registry, would issue such documents. This is the death certificate. Such a document, with this coat of arms of Bosnia Herzegovina like that, is the first time I have seen it. Nobody has died in my family, so I never went for such a document to be issued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have no further questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: There may be cross-examinations by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We will proceed in this way, first counsel for Mr. Delalic, second counsel for Mr. Mucic, third counsel for Mr. Delic and fourth counsel for Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, taking into account your previous decision, I would like to ask you whether I could ask the witness to talk to me as a counsel for Defence before I start with cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I told you I was not in a position to do that now. That was what I said. That would require postponing the cross-examination until each counsel had spoken to the witness, would it not? That will be the implication.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would only like to talk to him for some 10 minutes, and that would not prejudge the lengthening of this trial or the postponing of the cross-examination which I intend to do with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, I think that will be with the consent of the witness; is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Will you ask the witness whether he would wish to speak to counsel before he is cross-examined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That I hear. We can give him 10 minutes if he is willing to speak to counsel. We will rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is an extraordinary situation, since these witnesses had no opportunity to talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witnesses arrived last night at 9 o'clock. That was the earliest they could get here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In the meanwhile I suppose the witnesses can be asked whether they would like to talk to Defence or not. It is only if they agree that we can permit that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will undertake to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it seems to me that if all counsel want to speak to the witness then we should adjourn for sufficient time to permit that to happen rather than come in or come out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I believe you have two company directors relating to funerals. They can be finished in the meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As I understand it, counsel wants to speak to every one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Yes, they can. First we have to find out whether the witnesses will talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We will do that. The point I am making is if all counsel want to speak to this witness I suggest that 10 minutes probably would not be sufficient time, if it is going to be on the basis that they want 10 minutes to talk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: No, 10 minutes for all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is awkward. The first witness is willing to, I suppose, you can all meet him together, and discuss whatever you want to, because I do not think the Trial Chamber will be willing to give as many as 10 minutes to each counsel to talk to him, going in and out. I think it is necessary for the properness of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So far as this witness is concerned, I think 10 minutes for all counsel should be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that this matter be accounted fairly easily after we get through this first day. There will be lots of time this evening when these witnesses can be made available to us, those that will be testifying tomorrow. It may be that this can all be accomplished without interfering with the schedule of the Trial Chamber. I know it is a bit awkward this morning, but the witnesses have just arrived. I think it is fair we should be given the opportunity. I would appreciate the court's indulgence in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will rise and then come back at, let us say, 11.10 we should be back. (10.55 am) (Short break) (11.10 am)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, so far we have spoken to the next witness, Kemal Dzajic. He is prepared to speak to Defence Counsel. And we have spoken to General Arif Pasalic. He is prepared to speak to Defence Counsel on condition that there is a member of the Office of the Prosecutor, namely myself, there during the course of discussion with Defence Counsel. We have spoken to General Ramic and General Ramic is considering the matter. So far we have not been able to speak to General Divjak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This experience, we consider what we might do is that we will continue with the cross-examination now; and then all these other interviews can be made subsequently, not interrupt whatever proceedings we have. As long as the witness is prepared to speak to anyone I think he should have the opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am wondering what the Tribunal's pleasure is with regard to the normal 11.30 break. Mr. Landzo and Mr. Mucic were not allowed to leave the courtroom during this short break and so we are running up against some needs that they have. I just do not what you intend to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We could have had a 30 minutes break if we had no interruptions, and then returned at 12. That was the only break we should have had. I do not know; we might still continue until 1 o'clock and then break for lunch, except there is anything pressing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Landzo and Mr. Mucic were not allowed to leave the courtroom during the short break we just had. They have some biological needs we need to pay some attention to, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: They want to go to the bathroom, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose if you could spare us only five minutes we might then have a short cross-examination break and come back at 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is totally up to the Tribunal what you want to do with that. We do need one at some point fairly soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So we can have this witness and then we will break and come back at 12. During that period the Defence might be able, in co-operation with the Prosecution, to have the discussion with any other witness who is willing. This is not an order from the court, but merely observing whether the witness is willing to speak to the Defence. Ms. Residovic, can we have you continue for just five minutes? Then we will break.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours, for allowing me to contact, even though shortly, the witness. I would also like to thank the witness who was prepared to talk to Defence counsel for Mr. Delalic. Hello, Mr. Zebic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you know, my name is Edina Residovic and I am the Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Mr. Zebic, before I proceed with starting questions, I would just like to give you a warning, which is necessary in order that the Trial Chamber and all the others in the courtroom could follow what we are talking. We speak the same language, and I could ask a question to which you could answer very quickly. But interpreters there, sitting in the booths, cannot translate very quickly either what I say or what you answer. So, I would like to ask you to pay attention, through the headphones that are on the table next to you. Through those headphones you can hear the translation of whatever I say of all my questions into English. Only when this has been translated please answer. Have you understood that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Am I to change the headphones?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, do not change the headphones. What you are going to hear from the headphones is what I ask, on the ones that you have. The other headphones that are on the table, I am going to ask that the volume is increased, because this is the voice that all the people who do not speak our language listen to. Only when you hear that the translation has stopped, answer my question. Mr. Zebic, you came in front of this court after a subpoena has been issued, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mr. Zebic, that you were ready from the beginning to answer the communication of this court and come and appear in front of this court as a witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you were first asked by the people from the Office of the Prosecutor you gave your statement straight away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think you can continue at 12 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In the meantime they can talk, if the witness is prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I have told him that. The Trial Chamber will now rise and come back at 12.00. (11.30 am) (Short break) (12.00 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please remind the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic, you can continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Mr. Zebic, before we continue, may I draw your attention to the following: I shall try to make my questions brief and precise. I should like to ask you to try to answer them, also, as briefly and as concisely as possible, except when you feel that you need to make a clarification of importance for the Tribunal. Also, should you not understand the question, please feel free to ask me to repeat or re-phrase the question. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the break, you had just told the Trial Chamber, in answer to my question, that from the very beginning you were ready to co-operate with the Tribunal, and to make a statement at the Tribunal's request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of our conversation today, is it true that you told me that your wife is ill, and that your wife fell ill in the course of this last war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that it is very difficult for you, personally, to leave your wife for any length of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true to say, Mr. Zebic, that your wife finds it very difficult to cope with stressful situations, and that you are doing your best to protect her from such situations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, she has been warned by her doctor, her neuro-psychiatrist, that I should be with her as much as possible, that I should not leave her alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All these facts that you have now stated to the Tribunal, have you conveyed those same facts to the representative of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with the exception of this part about my wife. We did not discuss her.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zebic, did you ever refuse to testify before the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never refused to testify before this honourable Tribunal. At the beginning of September this year, I was called up from The Hague, I think it must have been by Ms. Wendy -- Wendy Lobwein, I hope I pronounce it correctly. We discussed the problem of my wife. I was supposed to appear at the Tribunal between 9th and 13th September, and I asked this lady to try, with the Registry, to inform the Tribunal of my situation, and I sent a fax requesting if my appearance could be postponed for a certain period, and forwarding all the physicians' findings from 1994 until this year, which was enclosed with this request.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zebic. Is it true, Mr. Zebic, that when you leave Konjic you have to leave your wife under constant medical care?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the reason why --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object to this. Your Honours, basically my objection is relevance. Of what possible relevance is this? If the witness wishes to address the Chamber in terms of challenging the subpoena on good grounds, that is entirely a matter for the witnesses. The witnesses may do that. It is not for Counsel for the Defence to take it upon themselves to abandon their appropriate responsibilities and then somehow or other appear to act for this witness. In my submission, this is irrelevant and I object to it on those grounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I continue with my cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think I share his view that it is completely irrelevant to what is here to see. You have your cross-examination, I agree. There are certain circumstances under which most other things not directly relevant could be asked, but I do not think this is necessary with this witness, because I am sure you are familiar with the efforts to get these witnesses, even to get them on video conferencing. I do not see the need for these questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, one of the basic rules of this Tribunal is to provide a fair trial and protection of the witness is an important part of our Code of Conduct before the Tribunal. As the Defence attorney of Mr. Zejnil Delalic, as an amicus curiae, I have put certain questions and I think in the interest of the protection of this and any future witnesses of any certain measures that may be taken against them, I think we, the Defence, have the right to put such questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Questions about his wife's illness and the difficulty of leaving her? Are those the questions you have the right to put.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, your Honours. I want to point out that this witness never refused to appear before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has already said that. Proceed further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He has said sufficient for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask my second question and last question in this area. Mr. Zebic, do you consider that there were no grounds for this measure to be taken against you on the basis of facts which were beyond your control?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I object to this question, your Honour, and I object to counsel appearing as amicus curiae. Amicus curiae: something to be granted with leave of the court to come before the court. This counsel is appointed to appear for her client, not as amicus curiae. I object to her putting questions on that basis. It is entirely inappropriate to pursue this line of questioning, notwithstanding your Honour has already pointed out the fact that you consider this line of question to be irrelevant. I object to this question and I object to the witness answering it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I simply rise in the support of the asking of these questions on this ground --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What grounds?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On this ground: pleadings were filed before this Tribunal within the last two weeks which indicated that the Officer of the Prosecutor had spoken with this man, that he had refused to come to The Hague and give testimony, and that he had said that the only way he would do that is by video link. I think a serious question arises as to whether or not the Prosecutor was being totally honest and truthful with this Tribunal in making those requests. I think that raises a serious matter that this Tribunal should be very concerned with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think that has been established sufficiently in his answers, that he had at no time refused to come and testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What he said was he was always willing to come testify. He asked for a postponement when asked to come in September. The Prosecution has advised you in their pleadings that he actually refused to come and therefore had to be subpoenaed and he would only testify by video link. Those things are true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Those are on record, it is not necessary to proceed like this. We have the records. It has been established. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will go on to some other questions. Mr. Zebic, as you have already answered to question of the Prosecutor, regarding 1992, when you held the position of general manager of the public utilities company, Standard, in Konjic, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also answered that this company engaged, among other tasks, in providing funeral services to all the citizens -- citizens of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please wait for the interpretation before answering my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zebic, throughout the time of the war you were in Konjic, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a citizen of Bosnia Herzegovina you are aware that on 1st March, 1992, a referendum for independence was held in Bosnia Herzegovina, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also know that all the citizens, all the inhabitants of Bosnia Herzegovina could have, if they wanted to, participate in that referendum and cast their vote?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also know, Mr. Zebic, that on the basis of the results of that referendum Bosnia Herzegovina was proclaimed an independent state on the 6th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you probably know, Mr. Zebic, that it was on that very day that the former JNA, with the assistance of various paramilitary formations from Serbia and Montenegro and parts of the Serbian population from Bosnia and Herzegovina, committed aggression against Bosnia Herzegovina, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Like the other citizens of Bosnia Herzegovina, you could have, thanks to Television Sarajevo, followed the developments in Sarajevo that look place in front of the assembly building of Bosnia Herzegovina which virtually meant the beginning of the unconcealed aggression on Bosnia Herzegovina. Were you able to see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did watch.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, Mr. Zebic, at that time you were actually in Konjic, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you were a witness of the fact that those events greatly disturbed and caused panic amongst the citizens who could not believe that such an aggression could be conducted against our country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were surprised.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As an inhabitant of Konjic you certainly know, and if you do please confirm this, that the town of Konjic was already in mid April 1992 virtually totally surrounded and that it was not possible to leave the town or get into the town, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first I was not aware of that. I was surprised later on when the aggression started and when the war began. I saw that we were indeed surrounded on the north towards Sarajevo and to the south towards Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But also, Mr. Zebic, on the east towards Lake Boridz and Nevesinje too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, clearly I forgot to mention that. I did not think that report was important, the route leading to Nevesinje. The Chetniks captured Lake Boridz and they reached the heights near Konjic, 5 kilometres from the centre of the city, the slopes of Borasnica and Kisera, from where they operated and shelled the town of Konjic. That is the southern and south eastern side.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You just said that this area in the direction of Lake Boridz, you did not think it was so important. Was that because the main road that you mentioned comes from the north, leading southwards, an area that you also mentioned and which is the only asphalt road linking Sarajevo to Mostar and Ploce?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore it is correct to say that Konjic is situated on the main road which is of vital significance for Bosnia Herzegovina and particularly for the town of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Both in terms of road and rail traffic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As an inhabitant of Konjic, you are also aware that the northern-most point of your municipality and this road leading to Sarajevo is the village of Bradina and through the tunnel, under Mount Istvan you pass from Herzegovina into Bosnia, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm before this Trial Chamber that intercepting the road at Bradina, or blocking the road at Bradina, would mean totally preventing the people of Konjic from reaching Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That goes without saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that on the southern and south western approaches to the town, 10 to 15 kilometres in the direction of Jablanica, Celebici and Donje Selo, which, if blocked, prevent leaving Konjic and going southwards, that is towards Zrebnica and Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Celebici is 6 kilometres on the rail and main road, and Donje Selo is 3 kilometres from Konjic on the railway line, without any stops in between.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zebic, in answer to the question of the Prosecutor, you said that your work -- you had a work assignment in your company, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that the War Presidency had restructured our activities and indicated the most significant assignments we had, and as the manager of the enterprise and according to the wartime schedule of assignments I got a decision on my work assignment, together with some other employees.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Zebic, you were aware of the fact that in the state of Bosnia Herzegovina the state of immediate damage was proclaimed already in the beginning of April, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis -- on that decision you do know, Mr. Zebic, that there was general mobilisation that was proclaimed in Konjic and the people of military age were not allowed to go out of the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you confirm in front of this Tribunal, Mr. Zebic, that these were normal decisions of the legal authorities of the municipality of Konjic, taking into account the fact of the immediate war damage -- the state of immediate damage of war that had been proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnia Herzegovina in it official gazette has proclaimed general mobilisation. On the basis of that official gazette the municipality of Konjic and its War Presidency had also proclaimed the state of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you, Mr. Zebic, confirm that your work assignment was in fact a military assignment, in a state of immediate war danger Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, specially because the activities that our company carried out were of special interest to our municipality. It was normal that such a state be proclaimed in our company, because, as one can see from the very name of our company, it was a public utilities company which was created by, established by, the municipality of Konjic. On the basis of that act we were all issued with a work assignment and we had to act in accordance with the requirements of the general interests of our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zebic, you have already mentioned that the attack on our country provoked a great surprise and panic. Could you please tell me as an inhabitant of Konjic, were you already in April -- have you heard, through Radio Konjic, the threats made by General Kukanjac that he would shell Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Every inhabitant of Konjic heard that, because it was on local radio and local television; and also the television and radio of Bosnia Herzegovina have also announced this threat of General Kukanjac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zebic, as you answered to the questions of the Prosecutor and you spoke about the conditions in which your company operated, you are certainly aware of the fact of the general conditions, the general state in which the town was, and you personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, you will allow me to show a video to the witness. These are video films made by the television that had been provided to the Chamber already a long time ago. I would like on the basis of this video to ask additional questions to the witness. I would like to ask the technical booth to show the video film number 1. At the same time, Mr. Zebic, I would like to ask you, in case you have a pen and a paper, please while you are watching the video could you note, in case you can see, what you recognise. (Video played)

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zebic, having viewed the video, could you now tell me, which town have you recognised on this video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My town, Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you have recognised the town of Konjic, could you please tell me, Mr. Zebic, whether the first part of the video-- this first video is the threat -- after the threat of General Kukanjac when there was general alarm and have you recognised --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have recognised the new and the old bridge. One of them was, the old one was destroyed in the Second World War and then reconstructed. This was the new bridge, as well as the junction in front of the university, the People's University.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After that one could see the cemetery. Could you please tell us whether you have recognised that part of the video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was our main cemetery in Konjic, and our company is managing that cemetery, and I recognised others, grounds. First the Muslim cemetery; next to it is the Catholic cemetery and later on towards the south east is the Orthodox cemetery, which is near the Catholic cemetery; and that is all -- in the part that we call Musala in Konjic. This is the cemetery called Musala.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zebic, on that video you also saw a date, the 4th May. Could you tell me, is it true that on 4th May the first shelling of the centre of the town started, when during those shellings there was a very strong shelling of the town cemetery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember it very well that first day of the shelling, the 4th May. I was in my office in the company, in my company; it is true on that 4th May, which I remember it very well, it was a Monday, on that day the shelling of Konjic started.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As the manager of the funeral company you know that on that same day the town cemetery was shelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zebic. Your Honours, as the witness has recognised the video, I would tender them as Defence exhibits and I would -- so I tender them. Has this exhibit been accepted?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In that case I would like to know the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video will be D70/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Zebic, could you confirm to this Trial Chamber that the shelling of Konjic after the 4th May continued with great intensity every day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you confirm that as a result of that shelling the town has been greatly destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was one of the towns of Bosnia Herzegovina which was mostly destroyed, especially the old part of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zebic, can you confirm that already in May there was a great number of wounded civilians and also dead civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because, of course, I was wounded myself at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zebic, if I tell you that according to the data of the hospital of Konjic, between 4th May to 26th May there were 27 civilians that came as casualties to the hospital, and also six civilians that had been killed; five wounded members of the TO, plus one member of the TO who had been killed; can you say that this data of the hospital of Konjic are correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to accept the correctness of these data, because it is an official institution which gave them, and that is the hospital, the hospital which took care of the wounded people, and also of the dead, because the dead people to start with were brought to the internal mortuary of the hospital, or else they were wounded so badly that they died in this mortuary of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless Mr. Zebic, you lived, at that time, in Konjic, and also had the job that you had. You could certainly confirm that certain persons that were killed, specially in the Serbian areas, were never brought to the hospital but were straight away buried by their family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the whole territory of the municipality there were such cases, especially later on during the conflict between the BiH army and HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you also agree with me, Mr. Zebic, when I say that a number of lighter casualties never asked any help from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that, but probably there were such cases. Yes, because when I was wounded there were ten of us that were wounded and two people were killed. I think two or three people never went to see a doctor at the hospital. These were just scratches, from parts of shelling and so on. There are probably such cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So on the basis of your personal experience that you have just given in front of this Trial Chamber you can confirm that in the period of the 1st -- that is 4th May, up to 26th May, the number of dead and wounded could have been even larger than the one given by the -- stated by the data of the hospital of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The municipality of Konjic is the fourth, by territory, the fourth largest in Bosnia Herzegovina. At that time it was very difficult to have relevant data for the whole territory of the municipality. So, probably it can be confirmed as a fact to be put in the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zebic, you have already said that as a result of the shelling the whole town was greatly destroyed, both the houses and the industrial facilities, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you can, Mr. Zebic, could you, please, assess whether what I know -- the facts that I have about the shelling are correct or not; that is, the facts that I was given by various people in Konjic. It was said that during 1992, on the town of Konjic, on average there were 60 shells that fell on the town every day, that there were days where several hundred shells were fired on the town, and there was one time they remember in 1992 when 600 shells were fired on the town. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I was the manager of a civilian company as simple inhabitant of Konjic, I can confirm the first part of what you have mentioned because when we were in cellars we were sometimes also counting the shells and trying to conclude when the shelling would stop, because there were indications saying if you could hear two shells being fired then there would probably be a third one. So that is something that I can confirm. And when it comes to these 600 shells that is something I heard recently at a meeting in Konjic. There was a round table that was held and there was a discussion about the aggression and so on and all the parties that participated in the election campaign discussed that. I only learned about that fact recently; but what is sure is that such days that happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, the results of the shellings were evident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have said, Konjic was among the towns that was destroyed the most. I think that Konjic is among the five, six or ten most destroyed towns in Bosnia Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zebic, I would like to show you once again some video clips, made by the Konjic television, which show certain events. So I would like you to watch those videos very carefully, note on a piece of paper whether you can recognise any of it, and then I would like to ask you some other questions. Could you please now show the video film number 3? (Video played) Okay. You can show also this part of the video as well. (Video played)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic, have you any particular thing in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was that after the video I could ask a few questions to the witness. As the video film has just ended and it might be time for lunch break then the questions I wish to ask the witness connected to this video may be asked after the break, if you agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a break for lunch and you can continue your cross-examination at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There is a matter I was going to raise your Honour, but I can do that immediately after the lunch break. (1.00 pm) (Luncheon adjournment) 19 20 21 22 23 24 25 (2.00 pm)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before this witness is brought in, I have a copy of a memorandum which I hand to your Honours. In fact I have two copies; one is a reproduction of the first original and one is a copy of the original. There is a copy there for your Honours, and one for the Defence. This is handed to your Honour to counter the allegation by Mr. Ackerman that I was dishonest and misled the Chamber in relation to this witness. I tender it for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But you act on instructions, it was not directed to you personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is what I would have thought, your Honour, but it was not the way in which I interpreted what he said; but I certainly do act on instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We attach no blame to you at all. In fact you can make a ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Would it be possible for us to see a copy, or each one of us see a copy of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I made a copy of that for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may continue you. Kindly remind him he is on his oath and then you continue with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zebic, immediately prior to the break, we saw a video. Do you remember what we saw before the lunch break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you, please, tell me whether you recognised the town on that video, and if you did tell us which?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognised Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the video clip you noticed the dates, the 6th and 9th May. So is it correct to say that these are video tapes from May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw the date on the screen, so I assume that that is the date and the town of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From your personal experience, you know that in the month of May the town of Konjic was shelled every day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell me, Mr. Zebic, in some greater detail, if you can recall, which parts of the town did you notice in the clipping that we saw, and also did you notice any housing, apartment blocks or any other buildings in the town of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The video showed almost all the district of Konjic, but I recognised most the main street, Marshall Tito Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you saw almost all the districts of the town of Konjic, is it true that in May, 1992, the town of Konjic was shelled all over, that is all its districts, and all it quarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I cannot give you a complete answer to that question, because there were parts of the town, such as the Boracko Jezero Street, known as the Luka, which is right next to the railway station, and the Herzegovina Brigada Street, known as Kolonija, and at the beginning of 1992 those areas were not shelled in May and June. I can assert this for Luka, because that is where I live.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But all the parts of the town shown in this video were shelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the exception of these two blocks, and the suburbs, particularly near Glavaticevo and Lake Borci.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To be even more precise, those two areas that you have mentioned were not shown on this video clip that we saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were not shown, close up, but if you show the new bridge then you see the area known as Luka and part of the Herzegovina Brigada Street; and it is true that there were no close-ups of these two areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As the witness has personally recognised the contents of the video, I would like to ask the Registrar to tell us the number of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is the same number as the previous one, 70. This time it will be B, 70B.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I should like to tender this exhibit as an exhibit of the Defence. Is it admitted, your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may, for what you think it should do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zebic, your enterprise, like the majority of enterprises in Konjic, was working under very difficult conditions in those days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The building where your company was housed was also shelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That was the reason due to which you had to move to another part of the building, that is the basement, as you told the Prosecutor, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the second half of 1992, your fixed assets were also seriously damaged, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact all your vehicles for the transportation of bodies were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By the end of 1993 they were all destroyed. When the war broke out between the HVO and the army of Bosnia Herzegovina our garage was immediately next to the front-line with the HVO, so that everything that was in the garage was torched with snipers or incendiary bullets. At the end of 1992, two hearses were destroyed. I already mentioned one. This was at the end of 1992. The other one was destroyed at the beginning of 1993. These are the exact data, based on our records. I am not talking about other vehicles, in other departments, which were also destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Zebic, that your workers often buried people, exposing their own lives to danger, at the risk of their own lives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was very difficult. Sometimes we carried out the burial at night, especially when the conflict with the HVO broke out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Mr. Zebic, since the period of interest to this Tribunal is the period from May to the end of 1992, not to enter into any other details that occurred later on, except if that is essential and linked to the events of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I accept the proposal. I was not aware of this fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In answer to a question of the Prosecution, you said that the municipal authorities, to be more precise the War Presidency of Konjic municipality, decided to set up a commission for burials, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, can you tell the court that in view of the shelling and the casualties that they provoked, there were cases of dead bodies or the wounded being left lying in the streets, or in apartments, so that efforts were made to give a dignified burial to all the dead, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should now like to ask your Honours, in view of the activities of this witness and his testimony, if we may show another video clip. This will be the last that I intend to show to this witness and I ask the technical service to show us clip number 5. (Video played) Mr. Zebic, there is some more, another minute, maybe. (Video played) Thank you. Mr. Zebic, after having seen these pictures, can you tell me whether you recognise the town that is being shown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is Konjic again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me any of the details that you recognise, which parts of the City?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This massacre that occurred, it was in the 15th September Street. I think that four persons were killed on that occasion, and our company provided all the services required. Then I saw Varda, where the Orthodox church is situated, which was also shelled, as could be seen. And finally I saw the Catholic church, and a line of citizens who were probably waiting for food; and in the premises of the convent of the Catholic church was where the Caritas Society functioned. It often distributed food to the citizens of Konjic, regardless of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You noticed the dates indicated on this video, and you also saw that it was July. Is it correct that these events took place in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After May happened, yes, in June, at the beginning of June, as far as my memory serves me, this case occurred then. I know, I recognise several people, somebody Mahmutovic, who that day came to visit his wife in Konjic, he got killed. Then Ljubovic, and the other two; unfortunately I cannot recall their names.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you also confirm that May -- like May, June, as well as the other months, were months of horror for the citizens of Konjic, that is a period of daily shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The intensity was the same from the 4th May onwards, except for these two districts that I mentioned, that is Luka and the 10th Herzegovina Brigade. The other areas were constantly exposed to shelling. The experts who are more knowledgeable about shelling, and I am not one of them, said that these were smaller calibre shells, and that they -- the -- they came from the village of Bijela, using mortars from 60, 80 and 120 millimetres, and that in particular these 60 and 80 calibre shells could not reach these two settlements.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Under these conditions, all the bodies of the municipality were operating. That is they were all working under very difficult conditions, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually people worked day and night to ensure the minimum requirements for people to be able to continue living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To be able to bury the people who were killed in this way in the streets, you said that a commission for burial was set up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the commission was composed of Jasna Dzumhur, Smajo Previjak, Zoran Kajlovic and Ivica Vidackovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I saw, on one occasion, the decision of the War Presidency at Jasna Dzumhur's.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zebic, I have here a rather poor copy of that decision; but since you have already had occasion to see it, would you please take a look at it, and tell me whether this is the decision you are referring to. The decision was disclosed to the Prosecution in January, by the Defence, and I have here a translation for your Honours, and for the Prosecution. This copy is very poor, and especially the heading is not very legible. We gave a better copy to the Prosecution and I will try to give a better copy for the Trial Chamber as well, in case this exhibit will be taken. Could you please have a better look at it? Could you, according to the contents of this document, recognise this is the document that you saw yourself, and that this is the commission you spoke about, answered by the Prosecutor, upon answer of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, this commission Jasna Dzumhur, Smajo Previjak and Kajlovic. I did not know the third person was Kajlovic. I also did not know Ivica Vidackovic was on that commission. He used to be the chief accountant in my company. But I know the signature of Mr. Hadzi Huseinovic, who used to be at that time the Chairman of the War Presidency. I suppose that this is real -- authentic decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, since the witness had previously spoken during examination-in-chief about this decision and that he recognised on this decision the signature of the Chairman of the War Presidency, and he also saw the decision in 1992, I think all the conditions are met for this decision to be admitted as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can admit it. What is the number?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
